facts: Sinclair argues aging should be treated as a disease: it is the common factor behind conditions from cancer to osteoporosis.
He criticises the disease-by-disease approach as extending lifespan but not healthspan, and says not classing aging as a disease misdirects research funding.
His Information Theory of Aging: loss of epigenetic information is the root cause.
DNA is the digital information and stays intact enough for cells to be reset to a youthful state.
The epigenome, for example methyl groups that block gene expression, is analog information whose predictable drift drives the hallmarks of aging.
Reviews trace the theory to yeast work in Leonard Guarente's lab, where DNA breaks made the Sir2 protein leave its post at the mating-type genes.
The book points to partial reprogramming with Yamanaka factors as a prospect, not a human treatment.

Caveat after the book: a December 2020 Nature paper from his lab put three reprogramming factors into retinal ganglion cells in mice and restored youthful methylation and better vision in a glaucoma model and in aged mice. Mice only.
Critics, including Charles Brenner in a letter to Cell, say the theory has not been tested.
scene_details: methyl groups sitting on DNA and blocking genes
the Sir2 protein leaving its post in yeast
the mouse retina in the 2020 paper
tension: If aging is one cause behind many diseases, why do doctors treat each disease separately, and is the cause really lost information?
opening_idea: Open on the contrast: every cell holds an intact DNA text, yet the layer that decides which genes are read has drifted.

lessons.idea: Ask what several problems share before fixing each one
lessons.anchor: disease-by-disease treatment versus one underlying cause; Everyday: a baker whose bread, rolls and cakes all come out dry and who adjusts three recipes before checking the oven

reflect_final: Which problem at work or at home keeps coming back in different forms, and what might those versions have in common?

use_cases.situation: A team lists three separate complaints that all arrive late
use_cases.move: Sinclair's argument is that one cause can sit under many diseases. Before we fix each complaint, what do the three have in common?

use_cases.situation: A relative keeps treating symptoms one visit at a time
use_cases.move: Sinclair says doctors chase one disease at a time. Could we write all the symptoms on one page and look for what links them?

use_cases.situation: You fix the same household issue for the third time
use_cases.move: Three repairs, same problem. I will stop patching and look for the one cause under all of them.

pocket_idea: Sinclair names one cause, lost epigenetic information, behind many ailments. Look for the shared cause behind problems that keep returning.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Sinclair says the DNA text stays intact while the layer deciding which genes are read drifts.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Sinclair calls aging a disease with one root cause: the cell keeps its DNA but loses epigenetic information, the marks that decide which genes are read. He says doctors fight one disease at a time and gain lifespan, not healthspan. Mouse work after the book restored vision in old mice, but it is mice, and critics say the theory is untested.
